reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / Manson's Tropical Diseases
clinicalPearls: Endemic to humid rural areas of Central and South America, especially Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela and Argentina, and typically affects male agricultural workers exposed to soil

Caused by the thermally dimorphic fungi Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and P. lutzii, acquired by inhalation of conidia; the acute/subacute (juvenile) form and the chronic (adult) form behave very differently
The chronic adult form is dominated by pulmonary disease with mucocutaneous lesions of the mouth, gums and oropharynx, often with a characteristic mulberry-like haemorrhagic stippling
The acute juvenile form presents with prominent reticuloendothelial involvement: generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and marrow involvement, and is more aggressive
Microscopy of pus, sputum or tissue classically shows the multiple-budding 'pilot's wheel' or 'Mickey Mouse' yeast form, which is diagnostic
Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation) supports diagnosis and helps monitor treatment response and relapse
Prolonged therapy with azole antifungals is standard for most cases, with amphotericin-based therapy reserved for severe or disseminated disease and long consolidation required to prevent relapse
reference.pathophysiology: Paracoccidioidomycosis follows inhalation of airborne conidia of Paracoccidioides species from contaminated soil in endemic zones. At body temperature the fungus converts to its pathogenic multiply-budding yeast form and establishes a primary pulmonary focus, which may remain latent for years or decades before reactivating, often when cell-mediated immunity wanes. A vigorous granulomatous response tends to contain infection in the chronic adult form, whereas an inadequate Th1 response permits lymphohaematogenous dissemination in the acute juvenile form. Chronic pulmonary involvement produces progressive fibrosis, and mucosal seeding gives rise to the destructive oral and laryngeal lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis (frequently co-exists and mimics the chronic form)
Histoplasmosis and other endemic dimorphic mycoses
Oral or laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
Lymphoma or other causes of generalised lymphadenopathy in the juvenile form
additionalInvestigations: Direct microscopy of sputum, mucosal scrapings or aspirated pus with potassium hydroxide preparation for multiple-budding yeasts
Fungal culture on appropriate media (slow-growing) with demonstration of dimorphism
Histopathology of biopsy material with special fungal stains showing the pilot's-wheel yeast
Serology by immunodiffusion or complement fixation for diagnosis and follow-up
Chest imaging to characterise the pulmonary infiltrates and fibrosis
Screening for co-existing tuberculosis and for HIV in atypical or severe presentations
redFlags: Progressive dyspnoea and respiratory compromise from advanced pulmonary fibrosis
Laryngeal or tracheal involvement threatening the airway
Disseminated juvenile-type disease with marrow failure or extensive lymphadenopathy
Central nervous system or adrenal involvement
Relapse or deterioration on treatment suggesting inadequate duration or immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: With prolonged antifungal therapy most patients improve, but chronic pulmonary fibrosis and mucosal scarring can leave permanent disability; the acute juvenile and disseminated forms carry higher mortality, and relapse is common if treatment is stopped early.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the chronic form as tuberculosis or cancer and delaying antifungal therapy
Stopping treatment when symptoms resolve rather than continuing prolonged consolidation, leading to relapse
Overlooking co-existing tuberculosis, which can worsen if only one condition is treated
Failing to recognise adrenal insufficiency arising from adrenal involvement
Not screening for underlying immunosuppression in unusually severe disease
